meta.title: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company: How Chairman and CEO C.C. Wei Is Defending the World's Largest Foundry Franchise — 2nm Mass Production Underway, CoWoS Advanced Packaging Capacity Doubling to Capture AI Silicon Demand, and a $165 Billion Geographic Diversification Drive Across Arizona, Japan, and Germany Reshaping the Geopolitical Calculus of Global Chip Manufacturing
meta.abstract: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC; NYSE: TSM; TWSE: 2330.TW) is the world's largest dedicated semiconductor foundry, commanding approximately 70 percent of global pure-play foundry revenue in 2025 and manufacturing the most advanced logic chips on the planet for every significant fabless semiconductor designer. Founded in 1987 by Morris Chang under the sponsorship of the Taiwan government, TSMC invented the pure-play foundry model — separating chip design from fabrication — and has since made that model the dominant paradigm of the global semiconductor industry. Under Chairman and CEO Dr. C.C. Wei, who assumed the dual role in June 2024 following Mark Liu's retirement, TSMC entered 2026 in its strongest competitive and financial position ever: fiscal year 2025 revenue reached US$122.4 billion, up 36 percent year over year, driven by explosive AI semiconductor demand that has made high-performance computing the company's largest end-market, surpassing smartphones for the first time. The company's 2nm (N2) process node entered volume production in Q4 2025 on schedule, with capacity already fully booked through 2026, principally for Apple's iPhone 18 Pro and a wave of AI accelerator tape-outs from Nvidia, AMD, and Broadcom. CoWoS advanced packaging — TSMC's heterogeneous integration platform enabling the multi-chiplet assemblies that power large language model inference hardware — saw capacity double to approximately 70,000 wafers per month by end-2025, yet demand continues to outpace supply. Simultaneously, TSMC is executing the most ambitious geographic diversification in its history: a US$165 billion commitment to build at least three fabs in Arizona, the first of which entered N4 production in late 2024; a joint-venture fab in Kumamoto, Japan (JASM) that began production in December 2024; and a Dresden, Germany fab (ESMC) targeting automotive and industrial customers for 2027 volume production. These initiatives have transformed TSMC from a geopolitically concentrated asset into a distributed global manufacturing enterprise, partially mitigating the Taiwan Strait risk premium that has historically discounted the stock. The dossier examines TSMC's technology leadership, financial trajectory, customer concentration dynamics, competitive moat, and the strategic tension between accelerating domestic expansion in Taiwan versus the operational complexity and higher cost structure of overseas fabs.

chapters.title: Strategic Snapshot: The Indispensable Foundry at the Center of the AI Chip Universe
chapters.body:
On the morning of April 16, 2026, C.C. Wei addressed analysts from TSMC's headquarters in Hsinchu and delivered a number that had never before appeared on a semiconductor earnings call: a 66.2 percent gross margin for the first quarter, the highest in the company's 39-year history. Revenue for the three months ended March 31 came in at [US$35.9 billion](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1046179/000104617926000199/a1q26e_withguidancexfinal.htm), up 40.6 percent year over year. Operating margin reached 58.1 percent. Wei's guidance for the second quarter — US$39.0 to US$40.2 billion in revenue — implied an annualized run-rate approaching US$160 billion. The figures were not the product of a favorable quarter in an otherwise cyclical business. They were the current-state expression of a structural position that has no parallel in the history of technology manufacturing.

## The Chokepoint at the Center of Everything

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company is the single most critical chokepoint in the global AI hardware supply chain. That position was deepening, not eroding, as the AI compute cycle accelerated through 2025 and into 2026. Every major artificial intelligence accelerator reaching data centers worldwide — Nvidia's Hopper and Blackwell architectures, AMD's Instinct series, the custom silicon powering Google's TPU clusters and Meta's training infrastructure — emerged from TSMC's fabs. The company held approximately 70 percent of the global pure-play foundry market by revenue in 2025, a share that was rising as Samsung Foundry's 3nm yield difficulties continued to cede ground at the leading edge.

[Fiscal year 2025 revenue reached US$122.4 billion](https://investor.tsmc.com/english/financial-data/financial-summary), a 35.9 percent increase in dollar terms versus FY2024 and more than double the company's FY2022 revenue base of US$75.9 billion. Net income for FY2025 approximated US$55.2 billion, implying a net margin of roughly 45 percent — a figure extraordinary for any company generating more than US$100 billion in annual revenue, and essentially unmatched in capital-intensive manufacturing. By May 2026, TSMC's market capitalization stood at approximately US$2.1 trillion, placing it among the five largest companies in the world.

The demand driver that produced these results was not the smartphone replacement cycle that had powered TSMC through most of its history. In Q2 2025, high-performance computing — encompassing AI accelerators, data center GPUs, and custom silicon for hyperscalers — surpassed smartphones to become TSMC's largest end-market, representing approximately 60 percent of wafer revenue by Q1 2026. The symbolic marker of this transition was Nvidia's ascent past Apple as TSMC's single largest customer in 2025, ending more than a decade of Apple's dominance atop the revenue ledger. Apple's A-series and M-series chips remained a franchise relationship representing an estimated 22–25 percent of FY2025 revenue, but Nvidia's insatiable demand for Blackwell GPU die and CoWoS packaging had, by the measures that matter most, redefined who TSMC's most consequential customer had become.

## Three Threads, One Thesis

The chapters that follow trace three interlocking narrative threads that explain how TSMC arrived at its current position and what it must execute to defend it.

The first is technology node leadership as competitive moat. TSMC's 2nm process node entered mass production in Q4 2025, on schedule and with yields that Wei characterized as favorable. The entire 2026 N2 capacity — ramping toward 100,000 wafers per month by December — was fully booked before a single wafer had shipped. No other foundry on earth has successfully ramped sub-5nm logic at commercial scale. Samsung Foundry's struggles at 3nm, and Intel Foundry's negative gross margins at current operating levels, have only widened the gap. The moat, built over three decades of process chemistry and EUV lithography expertise, is not replicable by capital expenditure alone, as the trajectories of both rivals demonstrate.

The second thread is CoWoS advanced packaging as the new strategic battleground. TSMC doubled CoWoS capacity from approximately 35,000 wafers per month in 2024 to roughly 70,000 by end-2025, and demand continued to exceed supply into 2026. The ability to assemble heterogeneous multi-chiplet packages — GPU die, HBM memory stacks, and networking silicon on a single silicon interposer — has evolved from a commodity service into a margin-accretive product that forces the largest customers in the world to commit capacity years in advance.

The third thread is geographic diversification as both risk mitigation and geopolitical accommodation. TSMC's US$165 billion commitment across Arizona, Japan, and Germany represents the most expensive capacity expansion in semiconductor history, dilutive to near-term margins but strategically essential: it is simultaneously a hedge against Taiwan Strait disruption, a response to government industrial policy on three continents, and a proof-of-concept that leading-edge fabs can be operated outside Hsinchu.

The tension at the heart of this dossier is whether TSMC can sustain the monopoly economics now visible in its income statement — the 66 percent gross margins, the pricing power, the customer lock-in measured in multi-year advance bookings — while absorbing the cost, complexity, and execution risk of the most consequential geographic expansion the semiconductor industry has ever attempted.

chapters.title: Corporate History: From Morris Chang's Pure-Play Gambit to the World's Most Valuable Manufacturer
chapters.body:
## The Founding Wager, 1986–1987

When Taiwan's government dispatched emissaries to recruit Morris Chang in 1986, semiconductor manufacturing was an industry organized around a simple axiom: companies that designed chips built them. Texas Instruments, Intel, and Motorola ran vertically integrated operations in which the design and fabrication functions were inseparable, each requiring the other's capital and expertise. Chang, then fifty-five, had spent twenty-five years at Texas Instruments rising to run its worldwide semiconductor operations before being passed over for the chief executive role. He was not an obvious candidate to overturn a global industrial paradigm. He did it anyway.

Chang's insight, which he later described as straightforward in retrospect but radical at the time, was that chip design and chip manufacturing were fundamentally different businesses with different capital structures, different talent requirements, and different competitive dynamics. If a manufacturer existed that designed nothing itself, it could serve every design house without competitive conflict and accumulate process expertise at a scale no vertically integrated rival would match. The Industrial Technology Research Institute, backed by Taiwan's government and its ambition to build a domestic semiconductor industry, offered Chang the mandate and the seed capital to test the hypothesis.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company was incorporated on February 21, 1987, in the Hsinchu Science Park. The Taiwan government held 48.3 percent of initial equity; Philips Electronics, which contributed process technology licenses and strategic credibility, held 27.5 percent. The remainder was placed with private Taiwanese investors. TSMC's first customer wafer deliveries came in 1988, produced on a single fab running a 2-micron process — a node that was, even then, trailing-edge by the standards of American and Japanese incumbents. The company began not with technological superiority but with a business model that neither Intel nor Motorola nor Samsung yet perceived as a threat.

## The 1990s: Scale, Philips, and the Fabless Ecosystem's Emergence

The model's vindication was slow but cumulative. Through the early 1990s, TSMC's growth tracked the concurrent explosion of fabless semiconductor design, a movement that its very existence was enabling. Companies such as Xilinx, Altera, and Broadcom — founded in the knowledge that they would never need to build a fab — became TSMC customers, validating Chang's premise. The Philips relationship provided both capital and a steady flow of technology transfer that helped TSMC close the process gap with IDM incumbents.

By the mid-1990s, TSMC had built out a multi-fab complex in Hsinchu and was investing in Tainan. Revenue crossed NT$10 billion. Chang, still chief executive, used the proceeds to fund successive generations of process development, establishing a pattern of reinvesting capital into technology leadership that would define the company for four decades.

## The 2000s: The 300mm Commitment and the Foundry Model's Coming of Age

The pivotal strategic decision of TSMC's second decade was the early commitment to 300-millimeter wafer fabs. Larger wafers produce more die per run and are essential to unit-cost competitiveness at high volume; the transition from 200mm to 300mm required billions in factory investment at a moment when the semiconductor industry was still absorbing the wreckage of the dot-com collapse and the 2001 recession. TSMC accelerated the transition ahead of competitors, opening its first 300mm facility in 2001 and expanding aggressively through the mid-2000s while rivals hesitated. The decision proved prescient: as the fabless model proliferated and volumes scaled, TSMC's manufacturing cost structure pulled ahead of any potential challenger.

In 2005, Chang stepped back from the chief executive role, becoming executive chairman — an acknowledgment that the company he had founded had grown into an institution complex enough to require dedicated operating leadership. His successor structure proved insufficient; by 2009, Chang had returned as CEO, a move he characterized as necessary to restore focus on technology execution. The interregnum nonetheless planted the seeds of the management bench that would eventually produce his successors.

## The 2010s: EUV, Apple, and the Consolidation of Leadership-Edge Dominance

The 2010s were the decade in which TSMC's competitive position transformed from substantial to structurally irreversible. The decisive turning points were two: the adoption of extreme ultraviolet lithography and the deepening of the Apple relationship.

TSMC committed to EUV lithography — a technology that uses 13.5-nanometer wavelength light to pattern circuits with a precision that conventional deep-ultraviolet tools cannot achieve — when the tools were still unreliable and expensive. The investments were enormous and the returns speculative. Intel, which had once been considered a decade ahead of TSMC, delayed EUV adoption, a decision that initiated the process leadership reversal whose consequences are still compounding as of 2026.

The Apple relationship evolved from a major account into something closer to a co-development partnership. Apple's A-series chips, beginning with the A9 in 2015 and expanding at every subsequent generation, demanded TSMC's most advanced nodes — 10nm in 2016, 7nm in 2018, 5nm in 2020, 5nm enhanced (N5P) for the A15 in 2021. The exclusivity, while never contractually confirmed, was functionally real: TSMC's yields and process density at leading-edge nodes consistently outperformed Samsung Foundry's competitive offerings. Apple's design ambitions required TSMC's manufacturing capability; TSMC's manufacturing investment required Apple's committed volume. Each reinforced the other.

| Node | First Production | Primary Early Customer |
|------|-----------------|----------------------|
| 10nm | 2016 | Apple / MediaTek |
| 7nm | 2018 | Apple A12, Huawei Kirin 980 |
| 5nm | 2020 | Apple A14 |
| 3nm | 2022 | Apple A17 Pro |
| N2 (2nm) | Q4 2025 | Apple (A20), MediaTek |
| Arizona N4 | Q4 2024 | Apple, Nvidia |

Mark Liu, who had joined TSMC in 1993 and risen through research and development, was elevated to co-chief executive alongside C.C. Wei in November 2013, establishing the leadership pair that would jointly manage the company through its most consequential growth phase. Chang formally retired in June 2018, ceding the chairman role to Liu. Wei assumed sole CEO authority simultaneously. Chang's retirement ended a thirty-one-year founding stewardship, but the institutional culture he had constructed — technology-first, customer-confidential, perpetual reinvestment — remained the operating system.

## The 2020s: Geopolitical Awakening, the AI Demand Surge, and the $165 Billion Expansion

The 2020 pandemic simultaneously exposed the world's semiconductor dependency and provided TSMC with the demand surge of its history. The post-COVID boom drove wafer prices to record levels as automotive, consumer electronics, and data center customers competed for constrained capacity. TSMC's revenue rose from US$45.5 billion in 2020 to US$75.9 billion in 2022, a pace that compressed what had been years of planned investment into quarters.

The boom's unwinding was abrupt. A global inventory correction in 2022–2023 reduced orders across mature and advanced nodes. TSMC's revenue dipped to US$69.3 billion in 2023, the first annual decline in years. What the correction demonstrated, however, was precisely the pricing power the pure-play model had generated: TSMC did not materially cut wafer prices to stimulate demand. Customers absorbed the inventory pain; TSMC's gross margins remained above 54 percent through the trough. The structural argument was vindicated by adversity.

The CHIPS and Science Act, signed into law in August 2022, provided the legislative framework for what became the largest geographic expansion in TSMC's history. The company had announced its first Arizona fab in May 2020; subsequent announcements layered on Fab 22 (targeting N3, 2027) and Fab 23 (N2/A16, accelerated to 2027 from 2028), bringing the committed US investment to US$165 billion. The US Department of Commerce awarded TSMC a preliminary CHIPS Act grant of up to US$6.6 billion in April 2024, the largest single award under the program.

In December 2024, TSMC Arizona Fab 21 entered N4 volume production — the first leading-edge semiconductor manufactured on American soil in decades. The milestone was more than symbolic: it demonstrated that TSMC's process discipline was transferable across geographies, answering a question the company's critics had used to argue the Taiwan concentration risk was permanent.

On June 4, 2024, Mark Liu retired after more than thirty years with the company. C.C. Wei assumed the chairmanship, consolidating both roles in a single executive for the first time since Morris Chang held them simultaneously. The structure — CEO and Chairman unified — was read by analysts as a deliberate signal of strategic continuity through a multi-year investment cycle that would not tolerate divided authority.

## The Founding Premise, Vindicated

In 1987, Morris Chang's argument was that separating chip design from chip manufacturing would create value for both sides of the transaction. By 2026, the argument had been proven to an extent that Chang himself may not have anticipated. Nvidia, whose GPU architecture drove the first generative AI wave, designs its Blackwell accelerators but manufactures every die at TSMC. Apple designs its own silicon but has never owned a fab. AMD, Broadcom, MediaTek, and Qualcomm — collectively responsible for the processing infrastructure of the modern digital economy — are fabless or fab-light by design. Every major AI chip company depends on TSMC as sole-source manufacturer at leading-edge nodes, a dependency so structural that disrupting it is considered a macro-level geopolitical risk, not merely a supply chain inconvenience.

The company that began on a single Hsinchu fab producing 2-micron transistors was, as of Q1 2026, generating US$35.9 billion in quarterly revenue — up 40.6 percent year over year — at a 66.2 percent gross margin, the highest in its history. The transistors it manufactured had shrunk from 2 microns to 2 nanometers, a dimensional reduction of one thousand times across thirty-eight years. The business model had not changed at all.

chapters.title: Technology Platforms and Product Lines: From Mature Nodes to 2nm and Advanced Packaging
chapters.body:
## Three Tiers, One Franchise

TSMC's technology portfolio spans a deliberate range from 90-nanometer specialty processes to angstrom-class nodes in development, and that breadth is architecture, not legacy. The company organizes its manufacturing around three distinct tiers, each serving different end markets, carrying different capital intensity profiles, and contributing differently to the consolidated gross margin that reached 66.2 percent in Q1 2026. Understanding the interplay among those tiers is essential to grasping why TSMC's revenue has proven more resilient than a pure leading-edge narrative would imply.

## The Foundation: Mature and Specialty Nodes

Processes spanning 90 nanometers through 16 nanometers accounted for approximately 30 to 35 percent of TSMC's wafer revenue as of early 2026. These nodes serve customers for whom process longevity, voltage tolerance, and regulatory qualification matter more than transistor density: automotive-grade SoCs certified to AEC-Q100 standards and guaranteed through decade-long vehicle programs, industrial microcontrollers, analog front-ends, and RF chips.

TSMC's geographic diversification was calibrated precisely to this segment. JASM in Kumamoto, Japan — 86.5 percent TSMC-owned, co-invested by Sony Semiconductor Solutions, Denso, and Toyota — entered volume production in December 2024, producing 22nm, 28nm, and 12/16nm FinFET wafers at approximately 55,000 wafers per month. Dresden's European Semiconductor Manufacturing Company targets 28nm and 16nm-class specialty processes for European automotive and industrial customers, with volume production scheduled for late 2027 backed by up to €5 billion in German government subsidies. Neither facility chases leading-edge nodes; both lock in automotive and industrial customers through long qualification cycles that make switching costs prohibitive.

## The Volume Backbone: N3 and Established Leading-Edge

The N3 family — N3E, N3P, and N3X variants — constituted TSMC's single largest revenue-generating node family in 2025. Apple committed to N3E for the A17 Pro chip in iPhone 15 Pro and the A18 series for iPhone 16, while Nvidia's Hopper H100 and H200 compute dies ran on N4, and AMD's EPYC server CPUs used N5 and N4 for compute dies. Seven-nanometer and five-nanometer processes collectively serve as the highest-output segment of TSMC's Taiwan fabs, with mature yield curves and largely depreciated EUV tooling delivering favorable cash economics.

| Technology Tier | Nodes | Production Status | Est. Revenue Share (Q1 2026) | Key Customers |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mature / Specialty | 90nm–28nm | Full production | ~30–35% | Automotive, IoT, analog, industrial |
| Established leading-edge | 16nm–7nm | Full production (HVM) | ~20–25% | Qualcomm, AMD, MediaTek |
| N3 family | N3E, N3P, N3X | Full production (HVM) | ~30–35% | Apple, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom |
| N2 | N2, N2P | Mass production (launched Q4 2025) | <5% (ramping) | Apple, MediaTek |
| A16 | N1.6 / A16 | Development / early tape-out | 0% | TBD (production 2027+) |

## N2: The Nanosheet Transition

The 2-nanometer node represents a more consequential architectural discontinuity than any transistor transition since the introduction of FinFET structures at 16nm. At N3 and above, TSMC used FinFET — a three-dimensional transistor in which the gate material wraps around three sides of a fin-shaped silicon channel. N2 abandons that architecture entirely in favor of nanosheet gate-all-around transistors, in which the gate wraps around all four sides of stacked horizontal silicon sheets that serve as the conducting channel.

The engineering significance extends beyond geometry. GAA structures allow device engineers to tune drive current by adjusting the width and number of individual nanosheets — a degree of customization unavailable in FinFET designs, where fin height is fixed by the deposition process. At equivalent power envelopes, N2 delivers approximately 10 to 15 percent greater speed than N3E; at equivalent performance, power consumption decreases by approximately 25 to 30 percent; transistor density improves by roughly 15 percent on logic macros. For AI inference accelerators operating continuously at data center scale, a 25 percent power reduction per die translates directly into reduced cooling costs and higher per-rack compute density — the kind of systems-level advantage that drives multi-year procurement commitments.

TSMC confirmed N2 entered volume production in Q4 2025, on schedule. By the Q1 2026 earnings call, CEO C.C. Wei characterized the ramp favorably:

> "N2 is progressing well. We are on track with our ramp schedule, and customer engagements remain very strong."

The entire N2 wafer allocation for calendar 2026 was fully booked at the frozen snapshot date — an unusual degree of forward visibility reflecting the multi-year design cycles of anchor customers. Apple committed N2 capacity for the A20 chip destined for iPhone 18 Pro, extending its unbroken streak of adopting TSMC's newest process for flagship products. MediaTek qualified as the second major N2 customer, targeting Dimensity mobile SoCs for premium Android handsets in 2026 and 2027.

The capacity ramp schedule ran from approximately 40,000 wafers per month at end-2025 to a targeted 100,000 wafers per month by December 2026, with longer-term plans extending toward 200,000 wafers per month as the node matures through 2027 and 2028. N2P — a performance-enhanced variant incorporating additional nanosheet optimization and improved local interconnect layers — entered customer tape-outs in 2026, with production volume anticipated in 2027. The ramp is constrained at multiple points beyond TSMC's direct control: ASML EUV tools are allocated years in advance, and the specialized process gases, atomic layer deposition chambers, and chemical-mechanical planarization equipment required for GAA fabrication make each capacity increment a coordinated supply chain exercise.

## CoWoS: The Packaging Bottleneck

No element of TSMC's portfolio has moved more abruptly from back-end commodity to strategic chokepoint than CoWoS advanced packaging. CoWoS — Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate — describes a family of integration architectures that assembles multiple semiconductor dies into a single package with interconnect densities far exceeding conventional printed-circuit-board assembly.

TSMC offers three configurations. CoWoS-S (Silicon interposer) places compute and memory dies side by side atop a passive silicon interposer that serves as a high-bandwidth interconnect substrate — the most mature and highest-bandwidth configuration. CoWoS-L (Local silicon interconnect bridge) substitutes an organic substrate with embedded silicon bridge chiplets, enabling larger overall package dimensions while reducing warpage risk and interposer cost. SoIC (System-on-Integrated-Chips) goes further, stacking dies vertically via direct copper-to-copper hybrid bonding with interconnect pitches measured in microns rather than tens of microns — enabling memory-on-logic configurations with bandwidth that conventional solder-bump approaches cannot match.

Nvidia's Blackwell architecture made CoWoS-S's constraints visible to the entire industry. A single B200 GPU package integrates two compute dies alongside twelve HBM3e memory stacks atop a silicon interposer approaching 800 square millimeters — the largest silicon interposer in commercial production. The GB200 NVL72 rack-scale system, combining 36 Grace-Blackwell Superchips in a unified memory fabric, consumes CoWoS at volumes that single-handedly constrained TSMC's packaging output through 2024 and into 2025. Broadcom's hyperscaler custom ASIC programs — Google's Trillium TPU, Meta's MTIA inference accelerator — contributed additional demand that reinforced the shortage.

TSMC responded by doubling CoWoS capacity from approximately 35,000 wafers per month in 2024 to approximately 70,000 wafers per month by end-2025. Management stated on the Q1 2026 call that demand continued to exceed supply even after that doubling, with dedicated CoWoS packaging facilities in Arizona under active planning. The supply constraint has forced customers to commit 12 to 18 months in advance — structurally improving TSMC's revenue visibility in packaging and creating a pricing environment where TSMC, not customers, sets the terms.

## A16 and Backside Power

TSMC's next node after N2 carries the designation A16 — the "A" prefix signaling angstrom-class geometry and a deliberate break from nanometer nomenclature. A16 combines a second-generation nanosheet transistor with refined gate dielectrics alongside backside power delivery network architecture, in which power rails are routed to the back face of the silicon wafer rather than sharing frontside metal layers with signal interconnects. The result is that frontside routing resources are freed entirely for data signals, improving routing density and reducing the IR-drop losses that degrade performance and efficiency in large compute dies.

Arizona Fab 23 — TSMC's third Chandler facility — was targeted for N2 and A16 production on an accelerated timeline of 2027, brought forward from an original 2028 schedule in response to US government and customer pressure. Customer tape-outs for A16 were expected to begin in late 2026.

## The PDK Lock

Process technology leadership is necessary but insufficient to explain TSMC's competitive durability. The deeper lock-in resides in the process design kit ecosystem — the libraries of validated IP blocks, standard cells, memory compilers, analog macros, and interface PHYs that third-party vendors certify against TSMC's exact process chemistry. Every SoC designer building on TSMC uses a PDK that encodes oxide thicknesses, dopant profiles, and contact resistance targets into the design rules and SPICE models governing circuit simulation.

Switching foundries requires not just re-qualifying a company's internal blocks but waiting for every third-party IP supplier in the bill of materials — ARM processor cores, Synopsys SerDes PHYs, Cadence memory compilers, dozens of specialty analog and interface macros — to complete their own re-characterization on the destination process. That aggregate timeline routinely exceeds two years even for well-resourced design teams. As each TSMC node accumulates a deeper library of validated IP, the penalty for switching grows. A16's PDK will inherit the investments already made by IP vendors for N2, accelerating its commercial ecosystem maturity relative to any greenfield node offered by a competitor. The PDK lock is the mechanism by which TSMC's process lead translates into customer retention that persists even when competitors narrow — or claim to narrow — the manufacturing gap.

chapters.title: Financial Deep Dive: Revenue Trajectory, Margin Architecture, and the Capital Intensity of Leading-Edge Dominance
chapters.body:
## A Revenue Baseline Without Precedent

Fiscal year 2025 delivered numbers that, even by the superlatives TSMC had accustomed investors to expect, stood apart. Full-year revenue reached NT$3,809 billion — US$122.4 billion at prevailing exchange rates — a 31.6 percent advance in New Taiwan dollar terms and 35.9 percent in US dollar terms over fiscal 2024. Net income for the year was NT$1,718 billion, approximately US$55.2 billion, implying a net margin of roughly 45 percent. To place that figure in context: very few companies generating more than US$100 billion in annual revenue have ever sustained net margins in that range, and none in manufacturing at anything close to TSMC's capital intensity. Diluted earnings per share for the full year were NT$66.26, or approximately US$10.65 per NYSE-listed American Depositary Receipt, each of which represents five ordinary shares.

The quarterly cadence inside that annual figure was perhaps the more instructive story. Gross margin widened from 58.8 percent in the first quarter of 2025 to 59.3 percent in the second, 60.4 percent in the third, and 62.3 percent by year-end, while operating margin tracked upward from 48.5 percent to 54.0 percent over the same span. This was not a single step-change driven by a price increase or a one-off gain; it was methodical compression of unit cost against a rising average selling-price mix — the signature of a company whose most advanced node was continuously maturing in yield while the next-generation node, with its richer pricing, was simultaneously being brought to volume.

The arithmetic of that progression arrived at a new high-water mark when first-quarter 2026 results were [reported on April 16, 2026](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1046179/000104617926000199/a1q26e_withguidancexfinal.htm). Revenue for the quarter was US$35.9 billion, up 40.6 percent year over year. Gross margin reached 66.2 percent — the highest in TSMC's history as a public company — and operating margin was 58.1 percent. Diluted EPS was NT$22.08.

| Period | Revenue (USD) | Gross Margin | Operating Margin | Net Margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 2025 | ~US$25.5B | 58.8% | 48.5% | ~41% |
| Q2 2025 | ~US$28.4B | 59.3% | 49.4% | ~42% |
| Q3 2025 | ~US$29.0B | 60.4% | 52.1% | ~43% |
| Q4 2025 | ~US$26.9B | 62.3% | 54.0% | ~45% |
| Q1 2026 | US$35.9B | 66.2% | 58.1% | ~53%+ |
| Q2 2026 (guidance) | US$39.0–40.2B | 65.5–67.5% | — | — |

Management's guidance for the second quarter of 2026 — revenue of US$39.0 billion to US$40.2 billion, implying a midpoint approaching US$39.6 billion, with gross margin of 65.5 to 67.5 percent — placed TSMC on an annualized revenue trajectory approaching US$160 billion. The numbers have compounded faster than most analysts dared model two years earlier.

## The Architecture of the Margin

Three structural forces explain why TSMC's gross margin has expanded so dramatically and why the trajectory is likely to persist at elevated levels.

The first and most powerful is **leading-edge node pricing power**. Advanced semiconductor nodes — 3nm, 2nm, and the coming A16 angstrom-class processes — carry wafer prices that are roughly two to three times those of mature nodes such as 16nm or 28nm. As the revenue mix has tilted toward leading-edge (driven by Apple's annual A-series and M-series chip transitions and by the explosive growth of Nvidia's Blackwell-family GPU programs), the average selling price per wafer across TSMC's installed base has risen structurally, not cyclically. High-performance computing, which encompasses AI accelerators, data center GPUs, CPUs, and networking ASICs, overtook smartphones as TSMC's largest end-market during the second quarter of 2025 and represented approximately 60 percent of wafer revenue in the first quarter of 2026. That shift in mix is, in essence, a secular ASP tailwind embedded in TSMC's revenue line.

The second driver is a **natural currency hedge** embedded in the cost structure. Roughly 70 to 80 percent of TSMC's revenues are denominated in US dollars, reflecting the global nature of semiconductor procurement contracts. The overwhelming majority of TSMC's costs — fab labor, local utilities, domestic engineering talent, and Taiwanese construction — are incurred in New Taiwan dollars. As the USD has strengthened against the NTD over recent years, each dollar of revenue has purchased more NTD-denominated cost base, mechanically expanding reported gross margin without any operational change. This is not a risk-free dynamic — a sustained NTD appreciation would reverse the benefit — but it has been a consistent tailwind in recent quarters.

The third driver is **operating leverage on fixed fab costs**. Semiconductor fabs are among the most capital-intensive fixed-cost structures in global industry. A fab does not cost materially more to run at 95 percent utilization than at 80 percent, which means revenue growth that drives utilization higher flows to gross profit at very high incremental margins. As demand for leading-edge capacity has outstripped supply across N3 and N2, TSMC's leading-edge fabs have operated near physical capacity constraints, allowing the fixed cost base to be spread across a growing wafer count.

Against those tailwinds sit three risks to margin sustainability. **Overseas fab cost premiums** are the most immediate: TSMC's Arizona operations carry structurally higher labor, construction, and energy costs than comparable Taiwan fabs. Management has acknowledged that overseas fabs will operate at gross margins below the company average during their early ramp years. **N2 yield ramp dilution** is the transitional risk — each new node generation temporarily compresses gross margin as engineers work to improve yields from initial qualification levels toward mature production targets. The N2 node entered volume production in the fourth quarter of 2025 and was confirmed by CEO C.C. Wei to be ramping with favorable early yields, but the dilution from a node at less than full yield maturity will persist into 2026 before recovering. **Technology node transition costs** — EUV tooling qualification, process development amortization, and customer tape-out support — front-load engineering expense in the periods immediately before a node begins generating revenue-scale wafer volumes. Each of these risks is transient by nature; none alters the structural margin architecture.

## Capital Expenditure: What US$52 Billion Buys

The capital expenditure trajectory is where TSMC's ambition becomes most legible. Capex was US$32.1 billion in 2023, rising to US$40.9 billion in 2025, and is [guided to US$52–56 billion for 2026](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001046179/000104617926000008/a4q25e_withguidancexfinal.htm) — a figure that exceeds the annual capital investment of any other semiconductor company by a substantial margin and rivals the capex budgets of the largest oil supermajors.

The deployment of this capital is occurring simultaneously across multiple geographies and technology programs. In Arizona, construction of Fab 22 (targeting N3-class processes) and Fab 23 (targeting N2 and the A16 angstrom-class process) is underway, with production from both fabs now accelerated to 2027 as part of TSMC's commitment to a US$165 billion total US investment. In Taiwan, the installation of extreme ultraviolet lithography tools for the N2 ramp — N2 is targeting approximately 100,000 wafers per month of capacity by December 2026, up from approximately 40,000 at year-end 2025 — is proceeding in parallel with CoWoS advanced packaging expansion, where dedicated capacity lines are being added to keep pace with AI accelerator demand. In Japan, Phase 2 of the JASM joint venture in Kumamoto is preparing for groundbreaking after infrastructure delays pushed the schedule, with production on 4nm to 6nm-class processes now expected in 2028 to 2029. In Germany, the ESMC fab in Dresden broke ground in August 2024 and targets 28nm and 16nm specialty production for automotive and industrial customers by late 2027.

| Year | Capex (USD) | Key Programs |
|---|---|---|
| 2023 | US$32.1B | N3 ramp, CoWoS buildout, Arizona Fab 21 construction |
| 2025 | US$40.9B | N2 EUV tooling, Fab 21 production ramp, Japan Phase 1 production, Germany groundbreaking |
| 2026 (guided) | US$52–56B | N2 capacity to 100K wpm, Arizona Fabs 22/23 construction, CoWoS expansion |

To understand the free cash flow equation, operating cash flow must be set against this capex. TSMC's operating cash flow generation has historically been robust — in excess of US$40 billion annually in recent years given the margin structure described above. At a US$54 billion capex midpoint for 2026, free cash flow will be compressed relative to 2025, a dynamic management has acknowledged and attributed specifically to the N2 ramp year. The recovery in free cash flow is expected as N2 yields mature in 2027 and wafer revenue per tool installation improves.

## Balance Sheet and the Government Subsidy Offset

Despite the scale of investment, TSMC's balance sheet has remained conservatively positioned. The company is net cash positive — cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments exceed total debt — with leverage ratios well below 0.5 times equity. Long-term debt is financed primarily through domestic corporate bond issuances and unsecured notes in the Taiwanese market, a conservative instrument set for a company with TSMC's earnings power. No material shareholder dilution has occurred through equity issuance; the capital structure has been funded through retained earnings and operating cash flow.

Government grants play a meaningful but not decisive role in the capex arithmetic. The US Department of Commerce, under the CHIPS and Science Act, awarded TSMC preliminary terms for up to US$6.6 billion in direct grants and up to US$5 billion in federal loans for its Arizona operations — among the largest CHIPS Act commitments made to any single company. The German government committed subsidies of up to €5 billion for the ESMC Dresden facility. These grants partially offset the higher construction and operating costs of overseas fabs but do not eliminate the structural cost premium; they function more as a risk-sharing mechanism between TSMC and host governments than as a profits subsidy.

## The Shareholder Contract

The financial chapter closes with the commitment management has made to long-term shareholders on dividends and returns.

In early 2026, TSMC raised its quarterly cash dividend by 28 percent, to NT$4.50 per ordinary share, with ADR holders receiving USD-equivalent distributions. That increase, arriving during TSMC's most capital-intensive investment cycle in its history, was a deliberate signal about management's confidence in the durability of free cash flow.

The explicit articulation of the long-term financial contract belongs to CFO Wendell Huang:

> "We believe a long-term gross margin of 56% and higher through the cycle is achievable, and we can earn an ROE of high 20s percent through the cycle."

At Q1 2026 gross margin of 66.2 percent, TSMC is running more than ten percentage points above that floor — providing a substantial buffer against the margin headwinds from overseas ramps and node transitions described above. The ROE commitment of "high 20s percent" on a capital base that will expand materially through 2027 as overseas fabs come online implies a net income trajectory that grows proportionally with assets, not one that stagnates as the equity base expands. That is a demanding standard. The quarterly results through the first five months of 2026 suggest TSMC is, at present, exceeding it.

chapters.title: Valuation: What the Market Is Pricing In — and Where the Bull, Base, and Bear Cases Diverge
chapters.body:
## A Multiple Unlike Any Foundry Before It

By late May 2026, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company's NYSE-listed ADR was trading in the US$422–430 range, anchoring a market capitalisation of approximately US$2.1 trillion and an enterprise value of roughly US$1.83 trillion after netting out the company's net-cash balance sheet. Those figures placed TSMC among the five largest companies on earth by equity value — a distinction that would have seemed implausible when the stock was changing hands at US$60 three years earlier.

The multiple table that accompanied that valuation was, by any historical standard for semiconductor manufacturers, extraordinary.

| Metric | TSMC (TSM) |
|---|---|
| Trailing P/E | ~31.8x |
| Forward P/E (2026E) | ~22–27x |
| Forward P/E (2027E) | ~21x |
| EV/EBITDA | ~18–20x |
| EV/Sales | ~14x |
| Price/Book | ~10x |
| Price/FCF | ~57x |

The P/FCF figure was the one analysts most frequently flagged as the fulcrum of the debate. TSMC's US$52–56 billion capital expenditure programme for 2026 — the largest single-year capex budget in the company's history — compressed near-term free cash flow materially, even as operating cash generation remained robust. The stock was, in effect, being valued on the expectation that the capex cycle would peak in 2026–2027 and that free cash flow would re-expand sharply as N2 yields matured and Arizona ramp costs moderated. Whether that expectation was realistic depended entirely on the trajectory of AI compute demand — and that, in turn, was the axis around which every scenario analysis rotated.

## History as a Reference Frame

The current premium becomes legible only against the arc of where TSMC has traded. Over the five years ending May 2026, the stock traversed one of the widest multiple ranges in its public history. During the 2021 peak of the semiconductor supercycle, TSM commanded a forward P/E of roughly 30–35x as consensus expected a sustained demand boom across every end-market simultaneously. The 2022 bear market punctured that optimism brutally: as inventory corrections swept through consumer electronics, smartphones, and PCs simultaneously, TSMC's forward P/E compressed to approximately 10–12x by October 2022, the cheapest valuation the stock had seen in over a decade, even as management insisted the AI capex cycle would eventually replenish demand. Investors who bought at those trough multiples saw the stock more than triple over the subsequent three years.

The 2023–2024 AI re-rating was the mechanism. As Nvidia's Hopper programme consumed an outsized share of TSMC's CoWoS advanced packaging capacity and N4/N5 wafer output, the market began to appreciate that TSMC had transitioned from a volume-sensitive cyclical into something structurally closer to an AI infrastructure monopoly with pricing power. The re-rating carried forward P/E from the low teens back through 20x and ultimately toward the current 22–27x range. By Q1 2026 — when TSMC posted US$35.9 billion in quarterly revenue, a 66.2% gross margin, and guided Q2 revenue to US$39.0–40.2 billion — the question was no longer whether the re-rating was justified in principle but whether the market had already fully discounted the upside.

## Peer Context

Placing TSMC's multiples in the context of its ecosystem peers clarified the premium embedded in the stock relative to both direct process-technology competitors and the downstream customers that depended on its output.

| Company | Fwd P/E (2026E) | EV/EBITDA | Rev Growth (2026E) | Gross Margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TSMC (TSM) | ~22–27x | ~18–20x | ~30%+ | ~63–66% |
| Samsung Electronics (SSNLF) | ~12–14x | ~7–9x | ~10–15% | ~35–40% |
| Intel (INTC) | NM / negative | ~18x | ~5–8% | ~38–42% |
| GlobalFoundries (GFS) | ~16–18x | ~8–10x | ~5–8% | ~27–30% |
| ASML (ASML) | ~30–33x | ~25–28x | ~15–20% | ~51–53% |
| Applied Materials (AMAT) | ~18–20x | ~14–16x | ~10–12% | ~47–49% |
| Broadcom (AVGO) | ~22–25x | ~17–19x | ~20–25% | ~67–69% |

Samsung traded at roughly half TSMC's earnings multiple, a gap explained in part by the conglomerate discount attached to its memory, consumer electronics, and display businesses, and in part by Samsung Foundry's deteriorating competitive position — external foundry market share had fallen to approximately 7% in 2025 against TSMC's roughly 70%. Intel's foundry operation was generating negative gross margins at current scale, making forward earnings comparisons essentially meaningless. GlobalFoundries, confined to mature nodes with structurally lower average selling prices, carried multiples more consistent with an industrial manufacturer than a technology franchise. ASML, the lithography equipment monopolist whose EUV tools were the physical prerequisite for TSMC's leading-edge advantage, commanded the most comparable premium to TSMC — a validation that the market was willing to pay scarcity rents for monopoly positions in the semiconductor supply chain. Broadcom, benefiting from the same hyperscaler ASIC boom that was filling TSMC's CoWoS lines, traded at a comparable forward earnings multiple with somewhat higher gross margins, reflecting the asset-light economics of custom chip design relative to wafer manufacturing.

The peer table told a consistent story: TSMC was not obviously cheap relative to its direct peers, but neither was it anomalously expensive relative to the other companies that enjoyed structural monopoly or near-monopoly positions in the AI hardware stack.

## What the DCF Implicitly Requires

No precise discounted cash flow estimate can be presented as authoritative given the range of assumptions involved, but the analytical variables the market was implicitly pricing at US$2.1 trillion were relatively tractable to bound. Working backward from that enterprise value with a WACC in the 9–11% range — reflecting TSMC's cost of capital adjusted for the Taiwan geopolitical risk premium that management repeatedly acknowledged was embedded in the ADR discount — and a terminal growth rate of 3–4% consistent with long-run nominal semiconductor demand growth, the implied free cash flow expectations were substantial. Consensus revenue CAGR assumptions for 2026–2030 of approximately 15–20% per year, combined with long-term gross margins sustaining above the 56% floor that CFO Wendell Huang had guided, were roughly necessary conditions to justify the current price under base-case assumptions. Any scenario in which revenue growth reverted to mid-single digits or margins compressed materially below 56% would require a much lower discount rate or terminal multiple to support the current equity value — an uncomfortable position for a stock already priced at 14x trailing sales.

## Three Scenarios and Their Price Implications

**Bull case — AI supercycle extension:** In the most optimistic scenario, the AI capital expenditure cycle among US hyperscalers extended without interruption through 2028, N2 node capacity unlocked a new pricing tier with average selling prices 20–30% above N3, and overseas fab productivity converged toward Taiwan levels faster than the sceptics expected — driven by CHIPS Act incentives and workforce maturation in Arizona. Under this construct, TSMC's revenue reached US$200 billion or beyond by 2028, gross margins sustained above 65% as N2 yield maturation repeated the pattern of N3, and the free cash flow inflection arrived earlier than consensus expected. The risk premium associated with Taiwan geopolitical uncertainty also compressed as the US-based production footprint provided partial economic insurance against scenario escalation. Under this framework, the TSM ADR carried potential to trade toward US$550–620 on a 24–26x forward earnings multiple applied to materially higher 2027–2028 EPS estimates.

**Base case — consensus execution:** The modal scenario assumed revenue growth of approximately 30% in 2026 — consistent with management guidance implied by the Q2 2026 revenue guide of US$39.0–40.2 billion — decelerating toward 15–18% annually through 2028 as the initial AI infrastructure build moderated. Gross margins sustained in the 60–63% range through the peak capex cycle before recovering toward 63–65% as N2 matured. The capital expenditure cycle peaked in 2026–2027 and free cash flow re-expanded meaningfully by 2028. Under this construct, the TSM ADR was broadly fairly valued at US$420–450, with upside and downside roughly balanced around execution delivery and the prevailing risk appetite for Taiwan-domiciled assets.

**Bear case — demand air pocket and risk premium expansion:** The downside scenario centred on two distinct but potentially correlated shocks. The first was a pause or moderation in AI hyperscaler capital expenditure — either from LLM training plateau concerns, inference efficiency improvements reducing per-query compute intensity, or financial discipline forced by rising interest costs on the cloud providers themselves. The second was geopolitical escalation in the Taiwan Strait that caused institutional investors to demand a materially wider equity risk premium for TSM's ADR, irrespective of underlying business performance. Compounding both risks was the possibility that overseas fab cost overruns — construction inflation in Arizona had already pushed project costs above initial estimates — permanently compressed blended gross margins toward the 56% floor rather than allowing them to recover above 60%. Under this convergence of headwinds, the TSM ADR could re-test the US$250–300 range, consistent with 12–15x compressed forward earnings — the kind of valuation last seen during the 2022 bear market trough.

## Growing Into a US$2.1 Trillion Valuation

At a US$2.1 trillion market capitalisation in May 2026, the market was implicitly discounting a compound annual earnings growth of approximately 15–18% for the better part of a decade, sustained gross margins well above the mid-50s percent, and a successful execution of the most geographically ambitious expansion in the company's history — simultaneously ramping N2 in Taiwan, N4 in Arizona, 22/28nm in Japan, and 28/16nm in Germany. Those were individually demanding tasks; executing all four in parallel, while maintaining the process discipline that had kept TSMC's technology leadership intact for three decades, was the central test of whether C.C. Wei's tenure would ultimately be judged as the inflection point that transformed a Taiwanese foundry into a permanent fixture of global industrial infrastructure.

The valuation implied that the market, on balance, believed he would succeed. What it did not fully price, by definition, was the left tail — the scenarios in which the geopolitical calculus shifted faster than the diversification programme could hedge it, or in which the AI capex cycle proved more episodic than structural. Those risks were priced partially, not fully, which meant the TSM ADR at current levels was neither obviously a gift nor obviously a trap. It was, instead, a precise bet on the durability of a monopoly that had never, in its four-decade history, failed to stay ahead of every competitor that tried to close the gap.

chapters.title: The Earnings Story: Quarterly Cadence, Management Commentary, and the AI Demand Signal
chapters.body:
## The Quarterly Call as Macro Barometer

Few corporate earnings events carry the systemic weight of TSMC's quarterly conference call. When Chairman and Chief Executive C.C. Wei and Chief Financial Officer Wendell Huang take the dial-in from TSMC's Hsinchu headquarters each mid-month, the audience extends well beyond holders of TSM ADRs: it includes the supply-chain teams of every major hyperscaler, the capital allocation desks of sovereign wealth funds, and the strategy units of every fabless chip designer on earth. TSMC reports its own results, but its customer roster — Apple, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, MediaTek, Qualcomm — means each quarterly update doubles as an unscheduled earnings preview for half the semiconductor complex.

Management provides guidance one quarter at a time: a revenue range and a gross margin range, nothing further. There is no full-year EPS guidance, no operating-income target, no explicit capex-versus-depreciation bridge. Analysts must build their annual models from this single quarterly data point plus whatever inference they can extract from management's tonal shift on AI demand, node-ramp progress, or packaging supply constraints. It is a deliberately lean disclosure philosophy that has the unintended effect of making each call disproportionately market-moving.

## Six Quarters of Uninterrupted Acceleration

The six-quarter stretch from Q4 2024 through Q1 2026 narrates a company moving from already-exceptional to historically anomalous.

**Q4 2024** marked the inflection point at which TSMC's Arizona strategy ceased being theoretical. Fab 21 in Chandler entered N4 volume production — the first leading-edge semiconductor manufacturing on US soil in decades — with Apple and Nvidia among the earliest customers to book wafers. Fourth-quarter results closed a fiscal year that had already begun rebounding from the post-pandemic inventory digestion of 2022–2023, and management used the call to signal that CoWoS advanced packaging demand was running structurally ahead of supply, a phrase that would recur with increasing urgency in subsequent quarters.

**Q1 2025** set the baseline for what would become a year of relentless margin expansion. Revenue came in at approximately US$25.5 billion — implied by the 40.6% year-over-year growth recorded in Q1 2026 — with a gross margin of 58.8% and an operating margin of 48.5%. Both figures were strong by historical standards but, in retrospect, represented the floor of a significant upward move. Sell-side analysts spent much of the Q&A pressing management on Arizona cost premiums; Wei's answer was consistent across multiple quarters: productivity at overseas fabs would converge toward Taiwan levels over time, and the geographic diversification was a strategic imperative that warranted a cost premium in the transition years.

**Q2 2025** supplied a structural milestone that will feature in TSMC retrospectives for years: high-performance computing, encompassing AI accelerators, data-center GPUs, CPUs, and networking ASICs, formally overtook smartphones as the largest end-market by wafer revenue. HPC's ascent to majority status had been visible in the trajectory for several quarters, but the crossing of the line was the formal marker that TSMC's business model had permanently realigned around compute infrastructure rather than consumer devices. Nvidia's Blackwell program — B200 and GB200 GPUs built on TSMC's N4 node and packaged on CoWoS interposers at scales previously unattempted — was the proximate cause.

**Q3 2025** saw gross margins continue their expansion as N3 node yields matured through the learning-curve improvement that management had flagged since N3's initial production ramp in late 2022. The NTD/USD exchange rate remained a tailwind: with roughly 70–80% of TSMC's revenue denominated in dollars and the bulk of its cost base in New Taiwan dollars, each incremental dollar strength added margin basis points without any operational change. Management again fielded questions about Samsung Foundry's competitive recovery trajectory; the answers were measured but the market-share data was unambiguous — Samsung Foundry's external foundry share had fallen to approximately 7% against TSMC's ~70% by 2025, and no near-term recovery was visible.

**Q4 2025** delivered what Wei described as the most consequential technology event of the quarter: N2 entered volume production on schedule. Gross margin reached 62.3% and operating margin 54.0%, demonstrating that even against elevated capital expenditure of US$40.9 billion for the full year, TSMC's operating leverage was intact. N2's initial yield performance was described as favorable — a notable departure from the early-N3 ramp, when yield issues had pressured margins for several quarters. HPC's share of wafer revenue continued to climb; the entire 2026 N2 capacity book was already full.

## The Analyst Interrogation Room

Across the six quarters, five recurring themes dominated the sell-side Q&A, and management's answers evolved in notable ways.

**CoWoS supply constraints** began as a capacity question — when would TSMC double packaging throughput? — and graduated into a strategic question about whether TSMC would build dedicated CoWoS facilities inside Arizona to serve US-based hyperscaler customers. Management confirmed the capacity doubling to approximately 70,000 wafers per month by end-2025 and indicated planning was underway for Arizona packaging infrastructure, without committing to a timeline.

**Arizona cost structure** evolved from skepticism to grudging acceptance. Early questions challenged whether Fab 21's cost per wafer could ever approach Taiwan levels given US labor costs and construction premiums. By Q4 2025, management was pointing to productivity improvements at Fab 21 and the CHIPS Act grant — up to US$6.6 billion in direct grants plus up to US$5 billion in loans — as meaningful offsets, and analysts had largely accepted that the cost premium would compress over time rather than persist.

**China revenue exposure** remained a recurring governance question, with analysts probing whether US export controls could curtail TSMC's Nanjing operations. Management answered consistently that Nanjing produces 16nm and 28nm mature-node wafers not subject to leading-edge export restrictions, and that Chinese customers' share of total revenue had remained contained. No guidance was provided on what a further tightening of export rules might do to that revenue stream.

## Q1 2026: History Made at 66 Percent

The Q1 2026 report, released April 16, 2026, was the most consequential quarterly result in the company's thirty-nine-year history. Revenue of US$35.9 billion exceeded consensus of approximately US$35.5 billion by a margin that individually would be unremarkable; what distinguished the quarter was the gross margin of 66.2%, roughly 300 basis points above the high end of management's prior guidance range — the highest quarterly gross margin ever recorded by TSMC or, for that matter, by any semiconductor manufacturer operating at comparable scale. Operating margin of 58.1% and diluted EPS of NT$22.08 against street estimates of NT$20.88 completed a clean three-way beat.

The beat versus guidance was driven by several converging factors: N2's favorable yield profile — favorable yields reduce wafer scrap and directly lift gross margin — accelerating HPC mix shift as AI customers consumed an outsized share of leading-edge capacity, and a USD/NTD exchange rate that continued to benefit the company's predominantly dollar-denominated revenue against its NTD cost base.

On the call, Wei offered the clearest articulation yet of why AI demand is structurally distinct from prior semiconductor cycles:

> "AI demand is extremely strong... The shift from generative AI and the query mode to agentic AI and the command and the action mode is leading to another step up in the amount of tokens being consumed."

The statement was significant not merely for its bullishness but for its specificity. Agentic AI — systems that autonomously plan and execute multi-step tasks rather than answer discrete queries — demands orders of magnitude more inference compute per user interaction than the original ChatGPT-era query-response paradigm. If Wei's characterization of the demand shift is correct, the silicon intensity of AI infrastructure is in an early chapter of a much longer expansion.

## One Quarter at a Time: The Guidance Philosophy

Wendell Huang's guidance framework shapes how the entire industry plans. By releasing only a revenue range and a gross margin range for the following quarter — and explicitly declining to provide full-year EPS guidance — TSMC forces analysts to work with imprecise annual estimates while concentrating information release into a single quarterly event. The practical effect is significant consensus dispersion on annual EPS, which in turn creates volatility around each call as the actual quarterly figures force model revisions in both directions.

Huang has anchored long-run expectations with a single durable commitment: gross margins of 56% and higher through the cycle. Against a current run-rate of 66.2%, that floor appears distant — but it constrains analysts from assuming current margins are permanent, and it acknowledges the reality that N2 ramp costs and overseas fab premiums will exert downward pressure in transition years.

## The Q2 2026 Setup

Management guided Q2 2026 revenue at US$39.0–40.2 billion, implying a sequential acceleration of roughly 10% from Q1's already-elevated base and an annualized run rate approaching US$160 billion. The midpoint of US$39.6 billion, if achieved, would represent year-over-year growth of approximately 38–40% — roughly in line with Q1's 40.6% pace, a remarkable feat given the size of the base.

A beat on Q2 guidance would carry a specific signal: that AI hyperscaler capex is not merely front-loaded into early 2026 but is durable enough to absorb a continuing supply ramp. A miss, by contrast, would raise questions about whether some portion of Q1's upside was pull-forward demand from customers building strategic inventory buffers against supply uncertainty. The answer will arrive in July, and the entire semiconductor investment community will be listening.

| Quarter | Revenue (USD) | Gross Margin | Operating Margin | Key Event |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 2025 | ~$25.5B (implied) | 58.8% | 48.5% | CoWoS supply constraints flagged |
| Q2 2025 | — | — | — | HPC overtakes smartphones as #1 end-market |
| Q3 2025 | — | — | — | N3 yields mature; Samsung share loss confirmed |
| Q4 2025 | — | 62.3% | 54.0% | N2 enters volume production on schedule |
| Q1 2026 | $35.9B (+40.6% YoY) | 66.2% (record) | 58.1% | Three-way beat; agentic AI demand signal |
| Q2 2026E | $39.0–40.2B (guided) | — | — | AI capex durability test |

*Sources: [TSMC Q1 2026 earnings release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1046179/000104617926000199/a1q26e_withguidancexfinal.htm); [TSMC Q4 2025 earnings release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001046179/000104617926000008/a4q25e_withguidancexfinal.htm); [TSMC investor relations](https://investor.tsmc.com/english/financial-data/financial-summary)*

chapters.title: Leadership: C.C. Wei, Wendell Huang, and the Board Governing the World's Most Critical Manufacturer
chapters.body:
## The Engineer at the Center of the World

When C.C. Wei addressed analysts on TSMC's first-quarter 2026 earnings call in April, he was speaking as the undisputed chief executive of the world's most consequential manufacturing enterprise — simultaneously fielding questions about 2-nanometer yield curves, CoWoS supply constraints, and the geopolitical calculus of a $165 billion overseas construction programme. That breadth of obligation would have been implausible for any single executive even a decade ago. It is now the job description Wei has carried since June 4, 2024, when the TSMC board formally conferred the chairman's title on him alongside the CEO role he had held since 2018, making him the first person since founder Morris Chang to hold both positions simultaneously.

The consolidation was not a surprise to anyone who had observed TSMC's governance closely, but its symbolism was unmistakable. Wei, sixty-four at the time of his elevation, had spent the prior six years quietly accumulating the credibility that justified it: engineering TSMC through the COVID-era demand surge, navigating the 2022–2023 inventory correction without a single leading-edge capacity write-down, and committing the company to the most ambitious geographic expansion in the history of the semiconductor industry.

## From New Haven to Hsinchu: A Career Built in Fabs

Dr. Che-Chia Wei's trajectory to TSMC's apex is, in miniature, the story of the global semiconductor industry itself. He earned a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from National Chiao Tung University — the same Hsinchu institution that has produced a disproportionate share of Taiwan's chip industry leadership — before completing a doctorate in electrical engineering at Yale University. His post-graduate career began at Texas Instruments in the 1980s, where he worked as a member of the technical staff in research and development at a time when TI was still one of the industry's dominant integrated manufacturers.

From TI, Wei moved through ST Microelectronics and Chartered Semiconductor, accumulating manufacturing operations experience across three distinct corporate cultures before joining TSMC in 1998. His first two decades inside the company were spent ascending through the fab operations hierarchy: Senior Vice-President of Operations I from 2005 to 2008, Senior Vice-President of Mainstream Technology Business from 2008 to 2009, and Senior Vice-President of Business Development from 2009 to 2012. The progression through operations, technology, and then commercial functions gave Wei a rounded command of TSMC's internal machinery that few outside the company fully appreciated.

The formal succession sequence began in November 2013, when Wei was elevated to President and Co-CEO alongside Mark Liu, with both reporting to founder Morris Chang, who had returned to the chairman's role in 2009. When Chang made his final retirement in June 2018, Wei assumed sole CEO responsibility, with Liu taking the chairman's title. The six-year interval between Chang's departure and Wei's assumption of the combined role created an interregnum of divided authority that the board ultimately judged had served its stabilising purpose.

What distinguished Wei's apprenticeship from a conventional succession — and what continues to define his leadership — is the absence of a financial or strategy background in his formative years. He is, at root, a process engineer who ran fabs. The implications are visible in how he manages expectations: his public statements on technology timelines, yield ramp curves, and capacity availability have consistently proved more reliable than those of peers at competing foundries, because he understands the constraints from the inside.

The geopolitical dimension of the role, however, has expanded in ways that no amount of fab operations experience could have prepared him for. Wei has met in person with American presidents, engaged European heads of government on the logic of the ESMC Dresden investment, and worked through complex trilateral negotiations with Japanese industrial partners including Sony, Denso, and Toyota on the JASM venture. His public communications on Arizona evolved markedly over three years: cautious acknowledgements of "cultural" and "skill" challenges in early earnings calls gave way, by 2025, to a more confident register.

> "We have much more confidence than last year that we can make it good progress," Wei told analysts on the Q1 2026 call, referring to the Arizona production ramp — a characteristically understated formulation that nonetheless marked a meaningful shift from the hedged language of prior years.

## Wendell Huang and the Financial Architecture

Where Wei provides the operational and strategic voice, Wendell Huang has functioned as the company's primary financial interlocutor with the capital markets for more than a decade. Huang, a 25-year TSMC veteran, has occupied the CFO seat through an extraordinary range of macro environments — from the chip shortage euphoria of 2021 to the inventory correction trough of 2022–2023 and the AI-driven surge of 2024–2026.

His central contribution to investor communication has been the articulation, and consistent reaffirmation, of two commitments that have become the analytical anchors for any financial model of the company: gross margins of "56 percent and higher through the cycle" and a return on equity of "high 20s percent." These commitments were established in a context of meaningful uncertainty — the early phases of the overseas fab buildout threatened to structurally compress margins, as offshore fabs carry meaningfully higher labour, logistics, and construction costs than their Taiwan counterparts. Huang's willingness to hold the floor regardless signalled that management believed the operating leverage of the AI demand cycle would more than offset the geographic cost drag.

The data validated the position. TSMC's Q1 2026 gross margin reached 58.8 percent — a figure that, while below the record 66.2 percent posted for the full first quarter of 2026, reflected a company operating substantially above its own stated floor even as it absorbed the early-stage costs of multiple overseas construction programmes simultaneously. The 56 percent floor, in retrospect, was set conservatively: it described a scenario in which AI demand normalised and overseas cost drag was at its most acute, a combination that has not yet materialised.

The ROE commitment carries different implications. Sustaining high-20s return on equity against a capital base expanding by $52–56 billion annually requires either exceptional margin performance, accelerating revenue growth, or both. In 2025 and early 2026, TSMC achieved all three simultaneously. Whether that combination persists through the completion of the Arizona, Japan, and Germany buildouts remains the central financial question the company faces.

## The Board: Governance for a Geopolitical Asset

TSMC's nine-member board is constructed around a clear principle: technical credibility over financial engineering. The board has no private equity representation, no activist investor, and no history of leveraged transactions. It is governed, in the relevant sense, by the people who built and run the semiconductor and technology industries.

The most consequential formal governance constraint is the presence of [Dr. Chun-Hsien Yeh](https://investor.tsmc.com/english/board-of-directors) as the designated Representative of the National Development Fund of the Executive Yuan — Taiwan's government-backed industrial investment vehicle, which holds approximately 6–8 percent of TSMC's ordinary shares. The NDF's board representation gives the Taiwanese government a direct, formal line of visibility into TSMC's strategic deliberations. The influence this creates is real but difficult to quantify precisely: it manifests not as veto power over specific decisions but as an informal constraint on the pace and scope of technology transfer to overseas facilities, the rate of leading-edge capacity migration outside Taiwan, and the terms on which foreign governments can access TSMC's most advanced processes.

The six independent directors bring a breadth of international credibility that serves TSMC's investor relations objectives almost as much as its governance ones. Sir Peter Bonfield, the former chief executive of BT Group, represents deep telecommunications infrastructure expertise. Michael Splinter, who served as chairman of Applied Materials — TSMC's single largest equipment supplier — brings an intimate understanding of the capital equipment market that shapes the company's capex planning. Moshe Gavrielov, the former chief executive of Xilinx, provides design-side perspective directly relevant to TSMC's largest customers as AI FPGA and ASIC workloads grow. Former MIT president Rafael Reif, a Venezuelan-American semiconductor researcher, connects the board to the US academic and policy ecosystem at a moment when CHIPS Act relationships are material. Ursula Burns, the former chairman and chief executive of Xerox, and Lynn Elsenhans round out the independent contingent with corporate governance and energy-sector expertise respectively.

## The Founder's Shadow

The most delicate governance dynamic TSMC navigates is one that appears nowhere in any proxy statement: the ongoing relevance of Morris Chang. Now in his nineties and retired since 2018, Chang has used public platforms to argue, with characteristic directness, that globalisation is "almost dead" and that the United States government is operating under a strategic illusion if it believes overseas TSMC fabs can substitute for Taiwan production.

The remarks created genuine diplomatic friction during the early stages of the Arizona negotiations. Wei's response has been to absorb the philosophical tension without resolving it publicly: he has never contradicted Chang, but has consistently presented the overseas expansion as a commercial necessity driven by customer demand rather than a repudiation of Chang's foundational thesis.

## The Succession Gap

The consolidation of the chairman and CEO roles in one person created a governance anomaly that the board has not yet addressed publicly. With Wei in his mid-sixties and no succession framework disclosed — neither a named deputy nor a formal timeline in any proxy filing — the continuity risk at TSMC is more concentrated than at any point since Chang's own retirement.

Historically, TSMC has managed succession through long internal apprenticeships: Wei himself spent twenty years inside the company before assuming its leadership. A similar pipeline presumably exists below him among the company's senior operational and technology executives. Whether the board's succession committee has formalised that process — and what it would look like to replicate the Wei-Liu co-CEO structure as a transition mechanism — remains one of the few material governance questions the company has chosen not to answer in public, even as it manages $165 billion in active construction commitments across three continents.

chapters.title: Customers and Markets: Apple, Nvidia, and the 300-Company Ecosystem That Runs on TSMC Silicon
chapters.body:
## The Concentration Paradox

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company's customer roster exceeds 300 names spanning every corner of the semiconductor industry, from hyperscale cloud giants to niche industrial chip designers. The breadth is real. The diversification is largely cosmetic. In fiscal year 2025, seven customers — Apple, Nvidia, MediaTek, Qualcomm, AMD, Broadcom, and Intel — collectively generated more than 60 percent of TSMC's US$122.4 billion in revenue. The top three alone, at roughly 42 percent of the total, produced a revenue stream that individually would rank among the world's largest semiconductor companies.

What this concentration figure obscures is why it does not translate into customer leverage over TSMC. Switching foundries at leading-edge process nodes is not a procurement decision; it is a multi-year engineering project. A fabless designer committed to TSMC's N3 or N2 node has built its IP blocks, design-rule-check flows, and physical verification toolchains to TSMC's process design kit. Migrating those designs to a Samsung Foundry or nascent Intel Foundry process requires 18 to 36 months of re-qualification, new tape-outs, yield development, and re-certification with downstream supply-chain partners. No customer of meaningful scale has executed that transition successfully at 5nm and below. The switching cost moat, not any contractual lock-in, is what lets TSMC extract leading-edge ASPs that carry two to three times the per-wafer price of mature-node work.

## From Consumer to Compute: The Apple-Nvidia Inflection

For more than a decade, Apple occupied a singular position in TSMC's customer hierarchy. The relationship predated the iPhone's dominance: Apple moved its A-series processor manufacturing to TSMC at the 28nm node and maintained that exclusivity through every subsequent shrink, from 20nm through 7nm, 5nm, 3nm, and into N2. By fiscal year 2024, Apple represented an estimated 22 to 25 percent of TSMC's annual revenue — a figure that understates the relationship's strategic depth, since Apple's designs consistently push each new node to production volume first, de-risking the ramp for every customer who follows.

That structural primacy began to shift in 2025. Nvidia, whose data center GPU shipments had been accelerating since the ChatGPT demand shock of late 2022, crossed into Apple's revenue territory during the year as Blackwell platform volumes ramped. Reports citing supply-chain analysis placed Nvidia ahead of Apple as TSMC's single largest customer by revenue in calendar 2025, though on a full-year basis the precise ordering remained subject to quarterly variation and Nvidia's share was estimated at approximately 11 percent of FY2025 revenue against Apple's 22 to 25 percent — a gap that reflects Nvidia's faster growth rate rather than Apple's decline.

The shift in the order of precedence was less important than what it signaled about end-market composition. Apple's silicon demand is bounded, ultimately, by global smartphone and personal computer unit volumes — markets growing at low single-digit percentages annually. Nvidia's silicon demand, in the AI infrastructure era, has been tracking exponential growth curves tied to data-center capital expenditure cycles at Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, and a tier of sovereign AI programs. The customer concentration numbers are, in this sense, a lagging indicator: Apple's percentage of TSMC revenue has not declined because Apple ships fewer chips, but because the denominator — total TSMC revenue — is growing faster than Apple's own procurement.

## HPC Surge: A Quantitative Map

The numbers underlying the HPC end-market ascent were among the most consequential in TSMC's operating history. In 2022, high-performance computing — encompassing AI accelerators, data center GPUs, CPUs, FPGAs, and networking ASICs — represented approximately 42 percent of TSMC wafer revenue.
